title: Francis and the birds
hook: a rich man's son gives it all away and preaches to the birds, who stay to listen (Little Flowers 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tolle lege: a child's voice in a Milan garden, and one verse. Your line was our heart is restless.

Assisi, a hill town in Italy. In front of the bishop and a crowd, a rich cloth merchant is furious with his son, Francis, who has been giving away the family's money and goods to rebuild a ruined chapel and feed the poor. The father wants it all back. So Francis takes off his clothes, every piece, and hands them to his father. From now on, he says, I can say freely, our Father who art in heaven. The bishop wraps him in his own cloak, and the party boy of Assisi walks out of town with nothing. Years later, on a road in the Umbrian countryside, he stops: the trees are full of birds.
screen: `A FATHER, A SON, A BISHOP.` → `HE HANDS BACK HIS CLOTHES.` → `TREES FULL OF BIRDS.`

segments.voice: One of his early biographers, Thomas of Celano, tells this, and the later Little Flowers of Saint Francis retells it with more color. Francis tells his companions, wait here, I'm going to preach to my little sisters, the birds. In the field he tells them they owe God a lot of praise: for their feathers, for the freedom to fly anywhere, for rivers and springs to drink from, for food they never had to plant or harvest, echoing Jesus's words about the birds of the air. And the story says the birds stay. They open their beaks, stretch out their necks, bow their heads, and don't fly away until he blesses them. Then they rise and scatter in four directions, like a cross. The Little Flowers mix memory with loving legend, and nobody knows exactly what happened there. But the heart of it matches his early lives: to him the whole world was family. Near the end of his life, sick and nearly blind, he wrote a song of praise in his home's Umbrian dialect, not church Latin: the Canticle of the Creatures. It praises God for brother sun, and sister moon and the stars, brother wind, sister water, brother fire, and our sister, mother earth. At the very end, he even welcomes sister death. Some churches bless animals on his feast day. A pope in our own time took his name, and titled a letter about caring for the earth with the canticle's refrain, praised be you.
screen: `MY LITTLE SISTERS, THE BIRDS.` · `THE BIRDS STAY TO LISTEN.` · `MEMORY MIXED WITH LEGEND.` · `THE CANTICLE OF THE CREATURES.` · then, large: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.`

segments.voice: Go to a window or step outside and watch a bird, any bird; a pigeon counts, a crow on a wire counts, and if there are none, a tree or the sky will do. Watch how it moves, how it lands; let it be your brother or sister for a minute. If you pray, praise God for it, the way Francis did; if not, just be glad it exists.
Little Flowers. The loving collection of legends about Francis, including his sermon to the birds.
Your line: brother sun, sister moon. Tomorrow, a nun from Ávila who laughed. That's ninety-three.

howItsDone: Saint Francis's feast day is October 4, and Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches often hold a blessing of the animals on or near it. The hymn 'All Creatures of Our God and King' is based on his Canticle of the Creatures.

chat.says: Did Saint Francis really preach to birds? Why do people love that story?
options: It mixes memory and legend, but its heart is true: to him all creation was family.
It's a proven event, written down word for word by people who stood there.
It's a later fable that has nothing to do with how Francis really lived.
chat.meaning: The Little Flowers mix memory with loving legend, but his early lives agree: to Francis the whole world was family, brother sun and sister moon.

notes: Date of the renunciation before the bishop: usually 1206; stated as 'around the year 1206'.
'From now on I can say freely, our Father who art in heaven' paraphrases the early lives (Celano, Bonaventure); not quoted. Confirm.
The Little Flowers are treated as memory mixed with legend; the Celano reference for the bird sermon should be checked (First Life, section 58).
Canticle of the Creatures: c. 1225; 'one of the first great poems in the Italian language' is a common claim; confirm.
Pope Francis (2013) and the encyclical Laudato si' (2015) are alluded to without naming; confirm this is acceptable on the broad Christian path.
'All Creatures of Our God and King' is W. H. Draper's paraphrase of the Canticle; it is named but not quoted.

Review fix: the script had said Laudato si' takes the canticle's 'first words'; the canticle opens 'Altissimu, onnipotente, bon Signore', and 'Laudato si'' is its repeated refrain. Changed to 'refrain, praised be you'. Confirm the English gloss.
'One of the first great poems in the Italian language' softened to 'often called'; 'party boy of Assisi' reflects Celano's account of his youth. Confirm tone.
